The logarithmic function. The inverse of an exponential function, written as log base a of x. It answers: what exponent do I raise a to in order to get x? Logarithms compress scales and convert multiplicative processes into additive ones, essential in science for measuring pH, decibels, and earthquake magnitude, and in computer science for analyzing time complexity. If a raised to the y equals x, then y equals log base a of x. The natural logarithm uses base e, written as ln of x, while the common logarithm uses base ten, written as log of x. The domain is the open interval from zero to infinity, and the range is all real numbers; the function is continuous and differentiable on its domain. Key properties include the product rule: log base a of xy equals log base a of x plus log base a of y. The quotient rule: log base a of x over y equals log base a of x minus log base a of y. The power rule: log base a of x to the n equals n times log base a of x. The derivative of ln of x is one divided by x, and the derivative of log base a of x is one divided by x times ln of a. The graph has a vertical asymptote at x equals zero, and for a greater than one, it increases unboundedly though slowly.
